title: A Renormalized Ginzburg-Landau Framework for Dimensional Crossover and Fluctuation Specific Heat in High-$T_c$ Superconductors in a Magnetic Field
authors: Roger Magloire Keumo Tsiaze, Jeremeie Edmond Danga, Cornelius Fai Lukong
abstract: This paper presents a theoretical analysis of phase transitions and critical phenomena in high-temperature superconductors using a renormalized Ginzburg-Landau framework. Rather than assuming a conventional linear temperature dependence, we treat the quadratic coefficient as a self-consistent, Hartree-renormalized quantity determined by fluctuation-loop corrections. This renormalization regularizes mean-field divergences and yields a finite, dimensionality-dependent specific-heat anomaly near the transition. When an external magnetic field is applied, minimal coupling quantizes order-parameter fluctuations into discrete Landau levels, reducing the effective dimensionality via an effective spectral dimension. In this framework, the intrinsic fluctuation-coupling strength self-consistently determines the temperature width of the critical Ginzburg region, while the cyclotron energy of the quantized fluctuations uniquely establishes both the specific-heat peak position and the upper-critical-field crossover boundary. Comparison with $\text{YBa}_2\text{Cu}_3\text{O}_{7-δ}$ experimental data demonstrates that this approach captures the suppression of the sharp mean-field discontinuity and accurately reproduces the vortex-lattice topological structure under finite magnetic fields.
summary: This work develops a renormalized Ginzburg-Landau theory to study superconducting phase transitions in high-Tc superconductors under magnetic fields. By self-consistently renormalizing the theory, the authors regularize divergences and accurately predict the finite, rounded specific-heat anomaly. This framework successfully models the dimensional crossover induced by the magnetic field, providing quantitative agreement with experimental data from YBCO.
main_problem: The paper theoretically analyzes phase transitions and critical phenomena in high-temperature superconductors, specifically addressing the limitations of standard Ginzburg-Landau theory in low-dimensional systems and under magnetic fields.
main_result: The renormalized framework successfully regularizes mean-field divergences, yielding a finite, dimensionality-dependent specific-heat anomaly that accurately captures the suppression and rounding of the mean-field discontinuity observed in cuprates.
method: The authors employ a renormalized Ginzburg-Landau framework, treating the quadratic coefficient self-consistently via Hartree-renormalization to account for fluctuation-loop corrections.
model_or_system: The system is high-temperature superconductors, modeled using an anisotropic-mass Ginzburg-Landau Hamiltonian. The theory incorporates minimal coupling to an external magnetic field, which quantizes fluctuations into Landau levels and effectively reduces the system's dimensionality.
key_observables: Fluctuation-specific heat anomaly, critical Ginzburg region width, specific-heat peak position, and upper-critical-field crossover boundary.
important_parameters: Dimensionality (D), magnetic field strength (B), and the fluctuation-coupling strength ($\eta$).
main_assumptions: The model focuses on orbital coupling, neglecting the Zeeman (spin-paramagnetic) pair-breaking term for simplicity. The analysis is performed in the long-wavelength, coarse-grained limit near $T_{c0}$.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the radial amplitude profile of an isolated vortex and the phase map showing the $2\pi$ phase winding characteristic of a singly-quantized vortex in 2D.
paper_structure: The paper builds from the standard GL Hamiltonian to incorporate renormalization effects, then extends this to include magnetic field quantization, culminating in the calculation of specific heat and vortex structure.
why_interesting: The rigorous treatment of fluctuation effects and dimensional crossover using renormalization techniques provides a powerful theoretical tool for understanding critical behavior in complex, layered quantum materials, which shares conceptual links with critical phenomena studied in AMO systems.

Application of a magnetic field suppresses superconductivity, thereby exposing the normal state and an extended regime of superconducting fluctuations. In contrast to the mean-field divergence anticipated in clean 2D systems for η = 0, the fluctuation-specific heat C2D fluc typically broadens without diverging and approaches the normal-state background at elevated temperatures.

Figure 1 presents data for a fixed B = 2.85 T and varying values of η = 0, 0.5, 0.9. The η = 0 curve serves as a robust validation, reproducing the sharp, near-divergent mean-field-like spike at Tc0 = 5 K, consistent with the prediction of Eq. (5) when fluctuation coupling is absent. Introducing nonzero values of η eliminates the divergence and reduces the peak amplitude (η = 0.5 to η = 0.9). This figure provides the strongest support for the central claim that η, independent of the magnetic field, regularizes the divergence. Figure 2. 2D fluctuation-specific heat at a fixed fluctuation parameter η = 0.5 as the magnetic field is varied: (a) ℏωc = 0.33 meV, B = 2.85 T; (b) ℏωc = 1.5 meV, B = 12.96 T; (c) ℏωc = 3 meV, B = 25.92 T. An external magnetic field breaks Cooper pairs, weakens superconductivity, and reveals thermodynamic fluctuation effects in 2D systems.

Figure 3. 3D fluctuation-specific heat at a fixed magnetic field (B = 12.96 T) as the fluctuation parameter η varies: (a) η = 0; (b) η = 0.5; (c) η = 0.9 (ℏωc = 1.5 meV throughout). Unlike the mean-field divergence expected for η = 0 in clean 3D systems, the fluctuation-specific heat C3D fluc usually broadens and approaches the normal-state background at higher temperatures.

Figure 3 presents data for a fixed magnetic field of B = 12.96 T, with η varying from 0 to 0.9. This figure extends the analysis of Fig. 1 into three dimensions. A divergence is observed at η = 0. Direct comparison of Figs. 1 and 3 indicates that the attenuation effect associated with η ̸= 0 in three dimensions is proportionally weaker than in two dimensions. This result is consistent with the physical interpretation that one-dimensionally confined fluctuations, which govern the 3D case under a field via r(1, T), are less restrictive than the zero-dimensionally confined fluctuations characteristic of the 2D case.
